design_detail: Randomized, counterbalanced, within-person crossover laboratory trial (Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit, Baltimore; June 2016 to January 2017) in 17 healthy adults who had not used cannabis for at least a month. Each person completed six 8.5-hour outpatient sessions at least a week apart: cannabis flower with 0, 10 or 25 mg of THC, either smoked in a small handheld pipe or heated in a desktop vaporizer (Volcano Medic) and inhaled from a balloon, over a 10-minute period. The three sessions of one method were run together; method order was counterbalanced across people and dose order randomized within each method. Described as double-blind, but no double-dummy was used, so people could tell smoke from vapor. Outcomes: ratings of drug effects (Drug Effect Questionnaire), three computerized performance tasks, heart rate and blood pressure, and whole-blood THC, at baseline and up to 8 hours after dosing. Registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03676166) after the study ended; the record was read.
can_establish: In 17 healthy adults who rarely use cannabis, in single laboratory sessions with one type of flower, one pipe and one desktop vaporizer, how ratings of drug effects, task performance, heart rate and whole-blood THC differed between smoked and vaporized cannabis containing the same THC in the material loaded, each person serving as their own comparison.
cannot_establish: How the two ways of inhaling compare when people pace and adjust their own use, in people who use cannabis regularly, or with joints, bongs, portable vaporizers, oil cartridges, concentrates or tobacco mixed in; how much THC actually reached the body (only the THC in the material loaded was set, not the amount delivered); anything about the lungs, repeated use or harm over time; differences by sex or between individuals (17 people); and, for most outcomes, whether a difference between the two methods is more than chance (only some contrasts were flagged, none was corrected across the 32 outcomes, and no interval is given for any of them).

sample.recruitment: Advertisements and word of mouth. Judged healthy by medical history, electrocardiogram, blood tests and physical examination; denied cannabis or other illicit drug use in the month before (timeline follow-back); urine toxicology negative for cannabis, amphetamines, benzodiazepines, cocaine, MDMA, opioids and phencyclidine at screening and before every session (Methods › Participants). Participants were paid. The registry record adds age 18 to 45, body mass index 19 to 36 and exclusion of non-medical use of psychoactive drugs other than nicotine, alcohol or caffeine in the 3 months before screening.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: As above. The paper defines infrequent use as no use in the past 30 days with a negative urine test; it does not state any minimum or typical earlier use beyond self-reported prior use of cannabis (Methods › Participants; Introduction, 4th paragraph).
sample.demographics: 9 men and 8 women; mean age 27.3 years (SD 5.7); mean weight 77.9 kg (SD 15.5), body mass index 26.2 (SD 3.3); 10 white non-Hispanic, 3 other or Hispanic, 3 black non-Hispanic, 1 white Hispanic. Mean 398 days (SD 437) since last self-reported cannabis use; median 365, range 30 to 1,825. How often or how much people had used before that is not reported.
sample.attrition: The text says 17 people completed the study and gives no count of people screened, enrolled or lost; the CONSORT flow diagram (Figure 1) is an image and was not extracted. The registry record gives actual enrolment as 18, so one person may be unaccounted for in the text.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers willing to inhale cannabis in a laboratory, abstinent for at least a month (a median of about a year) and screened for drug use before each session. People who use cannabis regularly, who may respond very differently because of tolerance, were excluded by design. Tiny sample; education, income, tobacco use and earlier patterns of cannabis use are not reported.

exposure.measurement: Study-administered. Cannabis flower from the US National Institute on Drug Abuse supply: batch 1 contained 13.4% delta-9-THC, 0.08% delta-8-THC, 0.03% cannabidiol and 0.8% cannabinol; the placebo batch contained under 0.01% THC with no detectable other cannabinoids. Target THC was set by weighing: 186.6 mg of placebo material for 0 mg, 74.6 mg of batch 1 mixed with 112 mg of placebo material for 10 mg, and 186.6 mg of batch 1 for 25 mg (the same amount of plant material in every session). Whole-blood THC was measured by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (limit of quantitation 0.5 ng/mL). Heart rate and blood pressure were measured seated with an automated monitor. Methods › Study Design and Procedure; Study Drug; Blood Specimens.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: 0, 10 or 25 mg THC in the plant material loaded; inhaled over a 10-minute period (smoked in a small handheld pipe prefilled and lit by the participant, with a metal top to hide the plant material and limit side-stream loss; or heated in a Volcano Medic desktop vaporizer at one fixed temperature, vapor collected in a balloon and inhaled until empty, three balloons for the 25-mg condition). Six single-dose sessions at least a week apart. Research pharmacy staff checked the pipe contents to confirm the whole dose was used; nothing was measured to show how much THC was delivered from either device (no puff, residue or exhaled-breath measure).
exposure.polysubstance: No cannabis or other illicit drug in the month before the study and a negative urine test and alcohol breath test before each session. Tobacco, nicotine and caffeine use are not reported. The pipe held only the study cannabis (no tobacco is mentioned).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 30 days by self-report at screening, mean 398 days; urine drug screens (rapid enzyme immunoassay) negative before each session. Blood THC before dosing is not reported.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant had all six conditions, including placebo cannabis (under 0.01% THC) smoked and vaporized, so every active condition is compared with the same person's placebo session of the same method, and the two methods with each other at the same THC content.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-person). Method order counterbalanced across people; dose order randomized within each method; the method of generating or concealing the sequence is not described.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Earlier frequency and amount of cannabis use, tobacco or nicotine use, expectancy about what each method would do, sleep, food and caffeine before sessions, and genetics (the authors say the sample was too small to examine such characteristics) were not measured or not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants in every condition; no illicit drug use in the month before and negative urine tests before each session.

outcomes.instruments: Drug Effect Questionnaire: 20 items rated on a 100-mm line from not at all to extremely (drug effect, pleasant, unpleasant, sick, heart racing, anxious or nervous, relaxed, paranoid, sleepy, alert, irritable, vigorous or motivated, restless, hungry, craving, dry mouth, dry or red eyes, memory impairment, throat irritation or coughing, difficulty performing routine tasks). Digit Symbol Substitution Task (number attempted, number correct, percent correct in 90 seconds), Divided Attention Task (time tracking the central stimulus, mean distance from it, peripheral stimuli correct out of 24) and Paced Auditory Serial Addition Task (correct out of 90, reaction time for correct and incorrect answers). Heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Whole-blood THC. Assessments at baseline and 0.17, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 hours after dosing (tasks not at 0.17 hours). Training on the tasks at screening.
outcomes.validity_norms: The tasks are described as sensitive to cannabis and relevant to workplace performance and driving, with references to earlier laboratory work (Methods › Outcome Measures); no norms or cut-offs for impairment are given. The authors conclude from this and other studies that blood THC is not a valid indicator of intoxication or impairment (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Effects and impairment are the peak change from each session's own baseline, compared with the placebo session of the same method (planned contrasts), and between methods at each active dose. No clinical, legal or safety threshold for impairment is set.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial. The two contrasts against placebo within each method used a threshold of P below .025; the two smoked-versus-vaporized contrasts per outcome (10 and 25 mg) were treated as orthogonal and tested at P below .05 with no correction; nothing was corrected across the 32 outcomes in the Table (up to 192 planned contrasts: 4 against placebo and 2 between methods for each), and Holm-Bonferroni was used for the correlations only.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants and staff were blinded to dose but not in practice to method: no double-dummy procedure was used, and an opaque bag over the balloons and a metal top on the pipe were used to hide vapor and plant material. Research pharmacy staff who checked the pipe contents were unblinded. Task scores, blood pressure and heart rate are automated; drug-effect ratings are self-report.

analysis.effect_sizes: Mean (SD) peak change from each session's baseline, smoked and then vaporized. Drug-effect rating (0 to 100): placebo 11.2 (15.9) and 2.1 (5.2); 10 mg 45.7 (26.4) and 69.5 (26.4); 25 mg 66.4 (28.6) and 77.5 (23.4). Heart rate (beats/min): placebo -3.7 (8.5) and -4.3 (6.1); 10 mg 11.3 (10.4) and 23.3 (11.8); 25 mg 19.1 (17.1) and 26.8 (16.6). Peak whole-blood THC (ng/mL), no placebo values given: 10 mg 3.8 (5.9) and 7.5 (5.5); 25 mg 10.2 (12.4) and 14.4 (9.4). Digit Symbol Substitution, number correct: placebo -3.2 (12.3) and +4.9 (8.9); 10 mg +3.4 (4.4) and -8.3 (11.3); 25 mg -7.0 (14.3) and -13.8 (14.9). Paced Auditory Serial Addition, reaction time for correct answers (ms): placebo -38.7 (107) and -43.8 (80.8); 10 mg +80.3 (119) and +86.9 (104); 25 mg +84.9 (90.8) and +85.4 (162). Between-method contrasts flagged at P below .05 in the Table: drug effect, dry mouth, dry or red eyes, vigorous or motivated, heart rate and Divided Attention mean distance at 10 mg; paranoid, vigorous or motivated, and Digit Symbol Substitution attempted and correct at 25 mg; also two Divided Attention outcomes in the 0-mg sessions. No interval or exact P value is given for any contrast. Editors' calculation (vaporized minus smoked difference in group mean peak changes; unpaired normal-theory 95% interval with t of 2.04, n = 17 per condition; conservative because it ignores the within-person pairing, whose correlation is not reported): drug effect at 10 mg +23.8 points (5.4 to 42.2; standardized difference about 0.9) and at 25 mg +11.1 (-7.2 to 29.4; 0.4); heart rate at 10 mg +12.0 beats/min (4.2 to 19.8; 1.1) and at 25 mg +7.7 (-4.1 to 19.5; 0.5); peak blood THC at 10 mg +3.7 ng/mL (-0.3 to 7.7; 0.65; ratio of means 2.0) and at 25 mg +4.2 (-3.5 to 11.9; 0.4; ratio 1.4). The paper itself reports no test of the blood THC difference.
analysis.covariates: Repeated-measures regression (first-order autoregressive covariance) with time, dose and method; no covariates, no period effect and no sex term reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03676166 was first submitted on 16 September 2018 and posted on 18 September 2018, about 20 months after the last session (17 January 2017, actual completion) and about two weeks before the paper was accepted (28 September 2018): a retrospective registration, so it cannot show what was planned. Registered primary outcome: quantity of THC in blood by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry, 8 hours after exposure. Registered secondary outcomes: Drug Effect rating, Digit Symbol Substitution, Paced Auditory Serial Addition and Divided Attention scores. The paper states no primary outcome; its headline findings are the ratings and task scores, with blood THC reported without a test of the method difference. Heart rate, blood pressure and the other 19 rating items are reported but not registered as outcomes. The record's summary also mentions oral fluid and urine, which this paper does not report. The trial protocol (Supplement 1, a PDF) was not opened.
analysis.selective_reporting: 32 outcomes in one Table with no correction across outcomes; the main text names the significant ones and reports the rest only in the Table; the sample-size reasoning is not about cannabis. Oral fluid and urine measures named in the registry summary are not in the paper. Adverse events are described in one sentence, with no counts for placebo or 10-mg sessions.
analysis.power: The authors justify 17 participants by a 1996 meta-analysis of six drug-administration studies of anti-anxiety medicines (about 14 participants each, effect sizes 0.87 to 1.0) published as a chapter in a government volume titled Problems of Drug Dependence (Methods › Statistical Analysis; reference 24). It concerns another drug class and other comparisons, and is not a power calculation for a smoked-versus-vaporized contrast or for blood THC, the registered primary outcome.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 17 healthy adults who had not used cannabis for a month or more, cannabis flower with 10 or 25 mg THC, smoked or vaporized, raised ratings of drug effect and heart rate and slowed or worsened some task scores in dose-ordered fashion, and effects outlasted blood THC (blood THC back to zero by 4 hours, heart rate by 3 hours, drug-effect ratings still above baseline 6 hours after the 25-mg conditions). With the same THC content in the material loaded, the vaporized condition had higher mean ratings of drug effect and a larger heart-rate rise at 10 mg, higher mean peak blood THC at both doses (untested, with wide spread between people), and more impairment on three flagged contrasts (Divided Attention distance at 10 mg; Digit Symbol Substitution attempted and correct at 25 mg). At 25 mg both methods raised ratings of unpleasant effects, anxiety, memory impairment and throat irritation or coughing over placebo, with no flagged difference between methods; two people vomited and one had hallucinations.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Key Points conclude that vaporized cannabis gave greater drug effects, impairment and blood THC than equal doses of smoked cannabis, that the 25-mg dose produced an increased incidence of adverse effects and significant impairment, and (Meaning) that the data should inform regulation of retail products and education. Gaps: (1) 'equal doses' means equal THC in the material loaded, not equal THC absorbed, and the explanation that smoking wastes more THC to combustion and side-stream smoke was not tested; (2) route differences were flagged for 4 of 20 rating items at 10 mg and 2 at 25 mg, and for 3 task contrasts, uncorrected and without intervals; the abstract hedges with 'qualitatively stronger' but the Key Points do not; (3) the blood THC difference has no test, and the editors' unpaired intervals include zero at both doses; (4) 'increased incidence of adverse effects' rests on three reported events (two vomiting, one hallucinations), all in 25-mg conditions, with no counts for other conditions; (5) smoked 25 mg differed from placebo on only some task measures; (6) the regulatory and educational implications go beyond a 17-person laboratory study. The abstract's headline numbers match the Table; the discussion is open about one dose range, one flower, one vaporizer and people who rarely use cannabis.

timeline.event: Abrams et al., a pilot study of vaporization as a smokeless delivery system, cited by the authors with two later studies by Newmeyer et al. (2016, 2017) as having found broadly similar blood THC and ratings of 'high' for smoked and vaporized cannabis (Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph). Not read here.

This trial: larger effects with vaporization at the same THC content loaded. The authors attribute the difference from earlier studies to those studies letting participants adjust their own dose, whereas this one required a fixed amount (Discussion, 2nd paragraph); that explanation was not tested.

replication.where_it_stands: One small trial in people who rarely use cannabis, which by its authors' account differs from earlier small studies. It has not been replicated in this card's evidence set. Read it as what happened with fixed amounts of flower in one desktop vaporizer and one pipe, not as a general ranking of vaporizing against smoking.

funding.funder: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), US Department of Health and Human Services. The paper states that the funder gave technical assistance on the design and conduct of the study, on analysis and interpretation of the data, and on preparing, reviewing and approving the manuscript, and had no role in collecting or managing the data. The cannabis was supplied by the US National Institute on Drug Abuse. Analytic testing of blood was done without payment by employees of Immunalysis Inc.
funding.declared_conflicts: Ryan Vandrey (senior author): personal fees, consulting or honoraria from Zynerba Pharmaceuticals, Insys Therapeutics, Battelle Memorial Institute and Canopy Health Innovations Inc, outside the submitted work; with Tory Spindle, SAMHSA grants during the study. Edward Cone: consultant for ConeChem Research LLC and RTI during the study. Nicolas Schlienz: National Institute on Drug Abuse grants outside the work. John Mitchell: SAMHSA grants. Eugene Hayes: funding from the Department of Health and Human Services, SAMHSA, the National Laboratory Certification Program and RTI International during the study. No others declared.
funding.affiliations_note: Two authors (Flegel, Hayes) are affiliated with SAMHSA's Division of Workplace Programs; the registry summary states that the study can inform policies on clinical, workplace and roadside drug testing, and the Discussion argues that blood THC is not a valid indicator of impairment. Other authors are at Johns Hopkins University and RTI International. The funder is a government health agency, not the cannabis or tobacco industry; one author has paid ties to cannabis and pharmaceutical companies (listed above). Read the funder's role in analysis and interpretation as a reason for closer reading, not for discounting.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized crossover study, registered before it starts with blood THC or impairment as the stated primary outcome, in people with different levels of cannabis use, in which people pace their own inhalation as in daily life, comparing joints, bongs, portable vaporizers and oil cartridges with the same product, with the amount delivered measured (exhaled breath, residue, puff pattern), a pre-specified analysis of the route difference with intervals, and sessions long enough to cover 8 hours of impairment.

domains.note: Method order counterbalanced and dose order randomized within each method, but how the sequences were generated and concealed is not described. The method comparison runs between two blocks of three sessions, with order balanced across people (17 cannot split evenly).

At least a week between sessions, urine tests negative for cannabis before each session, counterbalanced method order and training on the tasks. No period effect is modelled, and the Table flags smoked-versus-vaporized differences even in the 0-mg sessions for two Divided Attention outcomes, which shows session-to-session variation of a size comparable to some of the drug effects.

Described as double-blind, but the method cannot be hidden from the person inhaling, no double-dummy was used, and effects of 25 mg are perceptible, so expectancy may differ by method and by dose in the ratings. The dose was the THC content loaded, and neither device's delivery was measured, so the same label does not mean the same exposure.

17 people completed all six sessions. The registry gives enrolment as 18, and the flow diagram is an image (not extracted); a loss after a bad reaction would matter in a trial of this kind, but nothing in the text says that happened.

Blood THC, heart rate and task scores are objective, but the drug-effect and other ratings are self-reported by people who knew whether they were smoking or inhaling vapor, and the performance tasks depend on effort. One reported blood-pressure value is implausible (reporting issue 3).

Registered after the study ended; the paper names no primary outcome, though the registry lists blood THC; 32 outcomes with up to 192 contrasts and no correction across outcomes or for the between-method contrasts; no test of the blood THC difference; the protocol was not opened.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 applied as for a crossover trial. The within-person, placebo-controlled design protects against confounding between people, the exposure was administered and the main physiological outcomes are measured objectively. Four of six domains raise some concerns (sequence generation not described, blinding to method impossible, self-rated outcomes, late registration with many uncorrected outcomes); none is judged high. The source may be cited for what happened to 17 healthy adults who rarely use cannabis after fixed amounts of one flower in one pipe or one desktop vaporizer, including the dose-ordered effects of both methods and the higher mean ratings, heart-rate rise and peak blood THC (untested) with vaporizing at 10 mg. It may not be cited for a general ranking of vaping against smoking, for how people who use cannabis regularly respond, for the amount of THC delivered, for the incidence of adverse events, for the size of the blood-pressure or Divided Attention tracking-time changes, or for any effect on the lungs.

key_findings.finding: 17 healthy adults (9 men, 8 women), mean age 27.3 (SD 5.7), with no cannabis in the prior month (mean 398 days since last use, SD 437; median 365; range 30 to 1,825) each completed six 8.5-hour sessions at least a week apart: cannabis flower with 0, 10 or 25 mg THC, smoked in a small handheld pipe or vaporized in a desktop vaporizer (Volcano Medic) and inhaled from a balloon, over a 10-minute period. Sessions of one method ran together; method order counterbalanced across people, dose order randomized within each method.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Methods › Study Design and Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The flower was NIDA supply: batch 1 had 13.4% delta-9-THC (0.03% cannabidiol, 0.8% cannabinol); the placebo batch under 0.01% THC. The same weight of plant material (186.6 mg) was used in every session, with placebo material mixed in to give 10 mg. The 'dose' is the THC in the material loaded; delivery was not measured.
key_findings.note: The delivery caveat is the editors' reading of what was and was not measured.

key_findings.finding: Drug-effect rating (0 to 100), mean (SD) peak change: smoked 45.7 (26.4) at 10 mg and 66.4 (28.6) at 25 mg; vaporized 69.5 (26.4) and 77.5 (23.4); placebo sessions 11.2 (15.9) and 2.1 (5.2). All four active conditions exceeded their placebo (P below .025). Vaporized exceeded smoked at 10 mg (flagged P below .05); no difference flagged at 25 mg. Editors' calculation, unpaired, conservative: 10-mg difference 23.8 points (95% CI 5.4 to 42.2); 25-mg difference 11.1 (-7.2 to 29.4).
key_findings.locator: Table (Drug effect row); Results › Subjective Drug Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Abstract

key_findings.finding: Peak whole-blood THC, mean (SD) ng/mL: vaporized 7.5 (5.5) at 10 mg and 14.4 (9.4) at 25 mg; smoked 3.8 (5.9) and 10.2 (12.4). Peaks at the first sample (10 minutes) and back to zero within 4 hours in every condition. No test or interval for the difference between methods is reported; the smoked standard deviations equal or exceed their means. Editors' calculation (unpaired): ratio of group means 2.0 at 10 mg and 1.4 at 25 mg; difference 3.7 ng/mL (-0.3 to 7.7) and 4.2 (-3.5 to 11.9).
key_findings.locator: Results › Whole-Blood THC Concentrations, 1st paragraph; Abstract

key_findings.finding: Heart rate, mean (SD) peak rise in beats/min: smoked 11.3 (10.4) at 10 mg (not different from placebo) and 19.1 (17.1) at 25 mg; vaporized 23.3 (11.8) at 10 mg and 26.8 (16.6) at 25 mg; placebo sessions -3.7 and -4.3. At 10 mg the vaporized rise was larger than the smoked (flagged P below .05). Peak at the first measurement (10 minutes); back to baseline within 3 hours. Systolic blood pressure fell after smoked 10 mg (-10.1 mmHg, SD 23.9) against placebo; no other blood-pressure change was flagged.
key_findings.locator: Table (Physiological measures); Results › Physiological Measures, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Task performance, mean (SD) peak change. Digit Symbol Substitution, number correct: vaporized -8.3 (11.3) at 10 mg and -13.8 (14.9) at 25 mg, both below placebo; smoked +3.4 at 10 mg and -7.0 at 25 mg, neither different from the smoked placebo session (-3.2). Divided Attention, mean distance from the central target (pixels): vaporized 17.8 (23.0) at 10 mg flagged against placebo; the 25-mg value 35.4 (33.8) carries no flag in the Table although the text calls it significant. Paced Auditory Serial Addition, total correct: vaporized 25 mg -21.8 (24.9) only; reaction time for correct answers rose by 80 to 87 ms in all four active conditions. Smoked 25 mg also differed from placebo on Divided Attention time tracking. Between methods, flagged for Divided Attention distance at 10 mg and Digit Symbol Substitution attempted and correct at 25 mg. Deficits typically peaked 30 to 60 minutes after dosing and in some instances had not returned to baseline at 6 to 8 hours.
key_findings.locator: Table (Cognitive measures); Results › Cognitive and Psychomotor Measures, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Other ratings at 25 mg, both methods over placebo (P below .025): unpleasant (smoked 32.9, vaporized 24.4), anxious or nervous (21.4; 25.5), memory impairment (14.2; 16.2), throat irritation or coughing (27.8; 22.18), difficulty performing routine tasks (30.6; 34.2). Paranoid ratings rose over placebo only with vaporized 25 mg (17.4, SD 30.0, flagged above smoked 10.0); sick only with smoked 25 mg (20.3). Vaporized cannabis also raised dry or red eye ratings (19.2 at 10 mg, 25.1 at 25 mg). No difference between methods was flagged for unpleasant, anxious, memory or throat items.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table

key_findings.finding: Adverse events as reported: two people vomited (one after 25 mg vaporized, one after 25 mg smoked) and one had hallucinations after 25 mg vaporized. No counts are given for placebo or 10-mg sessions, and no other adverse events are listed.

Time course: after both 25-mg conditions mean drug-effect ratings were still above baseline at 6 hours (smoked 12.2, SD 5.9; vaporized 10.8, SD 4.4). Blood THC correlated with the drug-effect rating (r above 0.37) and heart rate (r above 0.24) in all active conditions, and with performance only for Digit Symbol Substitution correct at 25 mg vaporized (r = -0.32); the authors conclude blood THC is not a valid indicator of intoxication or impairment.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, 2nd paragraph; Results › Correlations Between Whole-Blood THC Concentrations and Pharmacodynamic Profiles; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that earlier controlled comparisons found similar profiles for the two methods, and suggest the different result here may be because those studies let people adjust their dose while this one gave a fixed amount, and that vaporizing delivers THC more efficiently because smoking loses THC to combustion and side-stream smoke (not tested here).

Limits stated by the authors: a limited range of doses, one type of cannabis (raw plant material, high THC and low cannabidiol), one vaporizer at a fixed temperature, enrolment limited to people who rarely use cannabis, and a sample too small to study individual characteristics. They note that the largest dose given (0.19 g at 13.4% THC) is smaller and weaker than the prerolls sold in dispensaries (about 1 g, often over 18% THC, citing a 2018 survey that was not read here).

Registry record NCT03676166: study start 16 June 2016, completion 17 January 2017, first submitted 16 September 2018, first posted 18 September 2018; actual enrolment 18; primary outcome quantity of THC in blood at 8 hours; secondary outcomes drug-effect rating, Digit Symbol Substitution, Paced Auditory Serial Addition and Divided Attention; masking listed as double (participant, investigator).
key_findings.locator: Study Registration Dates; Study Overview; Primary and Secondary Outcome Measures; Design Details

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that at 10 mg for both methods ratings of 'heart racing' and 'difficulty performing routine tasks' were raised over placebo (all P below .025), but the Table carries no significance flag for the smoked 10-mg values (4.2, SD 10.2, and 12.8, SD 27.7).
reporting_issues.consequence: The smoked 10-mg condition did not reliably raise these two ratings by the Table; the text overstates it. Use the Table.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says both vaporized doses worsened Divided Attention mean distance from the target (all P below .025), but in the Table only the 10-mg value (17.8) carries the flag; the 25-mg value (35.4, SD 33.8) does not.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a flag is missing or the text is wrong; the 25-mg value should not be quoted as significant until resolved.

reporting_issues.issue: Diastolic blood pressure after vaporized 10 mg is printed as a mean peak change of +40.6 mmHg with a standard deviation of 174.8, flagged as different from smoked; other blood-pressure entries have standard deviations of 6 to 25.
reporting_issues.consequence: Physiologically implausible: probably a data-entry error or an extreme outlier. The flagged blood-pressure difference between methods, and any statement about blood pressure with vaporized cannabis, cannot be relied on.

reporting_issues.issue: The Divided Attention 'time tracking central stimulus, %' outcome is printed as changes of -59 to -398 and 99, and the text restates differences from placebo as decreases of about 170%, 350% and 500%; a percentage of time cannot fall by more than 100 points.
reporting_issues.consequence: Units or definition unexplained. Quote direction only (flagged for smoked 25 mg and both vaporized doses), never the size.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table flags smoked-versus-vaporized differences in the 0-mg sessions for two Divided Attention outcomes (mean distance, total correct), so placebo sessions differed between methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: Session-to-session variation on this task is of the order of some of the flagged drug effects; the between-method Divided Attention contrast at 10 mg is the weakest of the three flagged performance contrasts.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Key Points say vaporized cannabis gave higher blood THC than equal doses of smoked cannabis, but no statistical test or interval is reported, and the smoked standard deviations (5.9 and 12.4 ng/mL) equal or exceed the means (3.8 and 10.2).
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction is consistent with the heart-rate and rating results, but the size is uncertain; the editors' unpaired intervals include zero at both doses.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Key Points state an increased incidence of adverse effects with 25 mg, but the Results list only three events (two vomiting, one hallucinations), all in 25-mg conditions, with no counts for other conditions and no test.
reporting_issues.consequence: The incidence claim has no numbers behind it. At most: three of 17 people had a reported event, each in a 25-mg session (each person had two 25-mg sessions, one smoked and one vaporized); none is reported for other sessions.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper says it followed CONSORT but gives no count of people screened, enrolled or lost in the text (Figure 1 is an image), and the registry lists actual enrolment as 18 against 17 analysed. The Table title was corrected on 21 December 2018 (wording of the Table title only, per the correction note).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether one person dropped out, and why, cannot be told from the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The sample size is justified by a 1996 meta-analysis of six studies of anti-anxiety drugs (reference 24, a chapter in a government volume), not by any cannabis study or route comparison.
reporting_issues.consequence: No evidence that 17 people were enough to compare smoked and vaporized cannabis; the many non-significant contrasts should not be read as no difference.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6324384 (all sections, the Table and author notes read as text; Figures 1 to 4 are images and their values were not extracted; Supplements 1 to 3 are PDFs and were not opened); ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT03676166 read for registration dates and registered outcomes
